questions.q: What tool would you use to accurately measure the "amount of turn" between two walls that meet at a corner?
questions.a: A protractor. If a student answers "ruler," they are confusing linear length with angular rotation, which is a common error because both tools are found in a geometry box.

questions.q: If a carpenter needs to ensure two pieces of wood are placed at a "right angle," what is the degree measurement they are aiming for?
questions.a: 90°. If a student says 180° (a straight line) or any other number, they have not yet grasped that a right angle represents a specific quarter-turn.

questions.q: You are asked to draw a path for a toy car that makes a 45° turn. How would you start this using a ruler and protractor?
questions.a: First, draw a straight line (the base ray) using the ruler. Place the protractor center on the start point, align the zero mark with the line, mark 45° on the paper, and then use the ruler to draw a line from the start point through that mark. Wrong answers often involve skipping the alignment step, revealing a misunderstanding of how to "zero" the tool.

questions.q: Compare the use of a ruler and a compass in construction. When would you need a compass instead of a ruler?
questions.a: A ruler is for measuring or drawing straight lines (distance), whereas a compass is for drawing arcs or circles (fixed distance from a point). A student might wrongly think a compass is just for drawing circles, missing its role in transferring equal distances or bisecting angles.

questions.q: An architect designs a window and says the corners must be 90°. If you measure one corner and get 85°, is the design correct? Why or why not?
questions.a: No, it is not correct because a 90° angle is a specific "right angle" required for square structures; 85° is an acute angle, which would leave the window frame skewed. This tests if the student understands that geometric precision is critical for physical stability.

questions.q: Design a simple "garden path" map on paper using two lines that intersect. How would you use a protractor to show the angle of the turn?
questions.a: The student should draw two intersecting line segments and place the protractor center at the intersection point to mark the degree of the opening. A poor answer would just draw random lines without defining the vertex or measuring the turn.
